title: History and Structure of the Earth
seo_title: Earth and Space Science 1: History and Structure of the Earth Worksheets (Strengthened SHS)
standard_code: Earth and Space Science 1, Quarter 1: Origin and Structure of the Earth
standard_text: Historical development of the Earth: formation, differentiation into layers, the early atmosphere and oceans, and the geologic time scale; structure and composition of the Earth's layers. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, Earth and Space Science 1, Quarter 1)
meta_desc: Free Earth and Space Science 1 worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Quarter 1): the formation of the Earth, its layers, the early atmosphere, the geologic time scale and dating rocks. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Earth is about 4.6 billion years old.
key_sub: Dense materials sank to form the core.
body_html:
How to think about it

The early Earth was very hot. Dense iron and nickel sank to form the core, while lighter rock formed the mantle and crust (differentiation). Volcanic gases formed the early atmosphere, and water vapor condensed into oceans. Photosynthesis later added oxygen.

The Earth's layers are the crust, mantle, outer core (liquid) and inner core (solid). The geologic time scale divides Earth's history into eons, eras and periods using fossils and radiometric dating of rocks.

Example

Which layer is liquid?

S-waves do not pass

Answer: the outer core

Example

Where did most of the oxygen in the air come from?

Living things

Answer: photosynthesis by cyanobacteria and plants

Common mistakes

  • Thinking the mantle is liquid.
  • Thinking the early atmosphere had oxygen.
  • Thinking humans appeared early in Earth's history.

faq.q: How do scientists know Earth's age?
faq.a: By radiometric dating of the oldest rocks and of meteorites.

faq.q: Why does Earth have a magnetic field?
faq.a: Movement of liquid iron in the outer core produces it.

items.q: What forms where two oceanic plates move apart?
c: a mid-ocean ridge with new crust
items.e: Magma rises to fill the gap.

items.q: Which layer is described: thin, rocky outer layer; thickest under continents?
items.e: Layers differ in composition and state.

items.q: Which evidence supports this claim: “The outer core is liquid.”
c: S waves do not pass through the outer core.
Earth's average density (5.5 g/cm³) is much greater than crust rock (2.7 g/cm³).
Seismic waves slow down in a zone about 100–200 km deep.
There is a shadow zone where no direct S waves arrive.
items.e: Match the evidence.

items.q: What is a mineral?
c: a naturally occurring inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and crystal structure
a substance made by living things
items.e: Quartz is SiO₂.

items.q: Evidence: P waves bend and slow down when they enter the outer core. What does it show?
c: The outer core is a different material and state from the mantle.
A liquid layer blocks S waves deep inside Earth.
The asthenosphere is hot and partly soft.
items.e: We learn about the interior mainly from seismic waves and density.

items.q: Which best describes Earth's crust?
c: thick layer of hot solid rock that moves by slow convection
thin, rocky outer layer; thickest under continents
liquid iron and nickel whose motion makes Earth's magnetic field
solid iron and nickel under enormous pressure
items.e: Match the layer.

items.q: Which process turns loose sediment into sedimentary rock?
items.e: Minerals cement the grains together.

items.q: Which layer is described: solid iron and nickel under enormous pressure?
items.e: Layers differ in composition and state.

items.q: How do we know the outer core is liquid?
c: S-waves (shear waves) do not travel through it, leaving an S-wave shadow zone
items.e: P-waves pass through but are refracted.

items.q: Which evidence supports this claim: “The asthenosphere is hot and partly soft.”
c: S waves do not pass through the outer core.
Seismic waves slow down in a zone about 100–200 km deep.
P waves bend and slow down when they enter the outer core.
Earth's average density (5.5 g/cm³) is much greater than crust rock (2.7 g/cm³).
items.e: Match the evidence.

items.q: What are the three main types of rock?
items.e: The rock cycle links them.

items.q: A basalt dyke cuts through sandstone layers. Which is younger?
items.e: Principle of cross-cutting relationships.

items.q: Which best describes Earth's asthenosphere?
c: thin, rocky outer layer; thickest under continents
solid iron and nickel under enormous pressure
liquid iron and nickel whose motion makes Earth's magnetic field
hot, soft part of the upper mantle that flows slowly
items.e: Match the layer.

items.q: About how old is Earth?
items.e: 13.8 billion years is the age of the universe.

items.q: Which rock is formed from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms?
items.e: Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate.

items.q: Which layer is described: liquid iron and nickel whose motion makes Earth's magnetic field?
items.e: Layers differ in composition and state.

items.q: Which best describes Earth's lithosphere?

items.e: Match the layer.

items.q: Evidence: S waves do not pass through the outer core. What does it show?
c: A liquid layer blocks S waves deep inside Earth.
The asthenosphere is hot and partly soft.
items.e: We learn about the interior mainly from seismic waves and density.

c: Much denser material, like iron, must be deep inside.
The outer core is a different material and state from the mantle.
The asthenosphere is hot and partly soft.
items.e: We learn about the interior mainly from seismic waves and density.

items.q: Evidence: Seismic waves slow down in a zone about 100–200 km deep. What does it show?
c: Much denser material, like iron, must be deep inside.
The asthenosphere is hot and partly soft.
A liquid layer blocks S waves deep inside Earth.
items.e: We learn about the interior mainly from seismic waves and density.

items.q: What is the principle of superposition?
c: in undisturbed sedimentary layers, the lowest layers are the oldest
the youngest layers are at the bottom
all layers formed at the same time
items.e: It gives relative ages.

items.q: Why do scientists use models of Earth systems?
c: because models are always exactly right
to simplify complex systems so they can be explained and predictions tested
items.e: All models have limitations.

items.q: A sample starts with 128 g of a radioactive parent. How much parent is left after 5 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 5 times: 4 g.

items.q: A sample starts with 320 g of a radioactive parent. How much parent is left after 2 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 2 times: 80 g.

items.q: A rock started with 64 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 5 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 64 − 2 = 62 g.

items.q: A piece of old wood has 1/8 of its original carbon-14 left (half-life 5,730 years). How old is it?
What drives the movement of tectonic plates?
c: the rotation of the core only
mantle convection, ridge push and slab pull
items.e: Slab pull at subduction zones is the strongest force.

items.q: A rock has uranium-235 and lead-207 in a ratio of 1 : 7 (half-life of uranium-235: 704 million years). How old is it? (Assume all the lead-207 came from decay.)
items.e: 1 : 7 means 1/8 is left → 3 half-lives = 2,112 million years.

items.q: A sample had 100 g of parent and now has 25 g. How many half-lives have passed?
items.e: 100 → 25 takes 2 halvings.

items.q: A rock started with 96 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 3 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 96 − 12 = 84 g.

items.q: A rock started with 320 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 3 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 320 − 40 = 280 g.

items.q: A rock started with 100 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 4 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 100 − 6.25 = 93.75 g.

items.q: Which layer of Earth is liquid?
items.e: S-waves cannot travel through it.

items.q: A sample starts with 100 g of a radioactive parent. How much parent is left after 4 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 4 times: 6.25 g.

items.q: A piece of old wood has 1/32 of its original carbon-14 left (half-life 5,730 years). How old is it?
A sample had 64 g of parent and now has 2 g. How many half-lives have passed?
items.e: 64 → 2 takes 5 halvings.

items.q: A rock started with 96 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 4 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 96 − 6 = 90 g.

items.q: A rock started with 80 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 5 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 80 − 2.5 = 77.5 g.

items.q: Rain falling on a mountain wears away rock and carries sediment to the sea. Which spheres interact?
items.e: Weathering and erosion link the spheres.

items.q: What is a reservoir (store) in an Earth system model?
c: a place where matter is held for a time, such as the ocean or the atmosphere
items.e: Fluxes move matter between reservoirs.

items.q: What is the evidence from fossils that life has changed over time?
c: fossils are found only in young rocks
different rock layers contain different fossils, with simpler life in older layers
all fossils are the same age
items.e: This is the principle of faunal succession.

items.q: How did cyanobacteria change the atmosphere?
c: their photosynthesis released oxygen, which slowly built up
items.e: This led to the Great Oxidation Event.

items.q: Which gases made up most of Earth's early atmosphere?
c: carbon dioxide, water vapor and nitrogen, from volcanic outgassing
items.e: There was almost no free oxygen.

items.q: Why did early Earth's oceans contain lots of dissolved iron?
c: there was almost no oxygen, so iron stayed dissolved
items.e: Oxygen later made it precipitate as iron oxide.

items.q: What is a mass extinction?
c: the loss of a large proportion of species in a geologically short time
the slow extinction of one species
items.e: There have been five major mass extinctions.

items.q: What is coevolution of life and Earth?
c: life changes Earth's systems, and those changes in turn affect how life evolves
life and Earth never affect each other
items.e: Oxygen from life allowed animals to evolve.

items.q: How did the evolution of land plants affect the atmosphere about 400 million years ago?
c: they removed large amounts of CO₂ and helped cool the climate

items.q: Which evidence suggests Earth's earliest life lived in the oceans?

items.q: What are red beds, and what do they show?
c: land sediments colored by iron oxides, showing oxygen was present in the atmosphere

items.q: Why are cyanobacteria called 'the organisms that changed the world'?

items.q: Which came first: the first complex (eukaryotic) cells, or the first oxygen-making cyanobacteria?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: The first oxygen-making cyanobacteria: about 2.7 billion years ago; the first complex (eukaryotic) cells: about 1.8 billion years ago.

items.q: Dennis's timeline lists this event: Earth forms (4,600 million years ago). In which part of the time scale did it happen? (Paleozoic: 541–252, Mesozoic: 252–66, Cenozoic: 66–now, in millions of years ago)
items.e: Earth forms 4,600 million years ago falls in the Precambrian.

items.q: Diane observes in a cliff: “A worn, uneven surface (an unconformity) lies between two sets of layers.” What can be concluded?
c: The fault happened after A, B and C formed but before D.
The granite is older than the sandstone.
Some rock was eroded away, so part of the record is missing.
The two layers formed at about the same time (an index fossil).
items.e: Relative dating uses superposition, cross-cutting features, unconformities, inclusions and index fossils.
